title: Solve Linear Inequalities: Boundary and Test
description: Solve linear inequalities in one variable and test values or ordered pairs in inequalities with two variables.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep your first idea, even if you are unsure. You can continue without submitting an answer.

shared_prompt.title: Opening question
shared_prompt.html: Solve \(7-4(2x-1)>27\). What is the greatest integer value of \(x\) that satisfies the inequality?

blocks.html:
Keep track of the allowed side

The opening question needs more than the value at equality: it asks which integers are allowed. We’ll use Boundary and Test to track that range.

First, look at why multiplying by a negative changes an inequality’s direction.

Watch the order reverse

Start with 2<5. Multiplying both by -1 gives -2 and -5. Since -2 is greater than -5, the true statement is -2>-5.

content.prompt: If \(3<7\), which statement is true after both sides are multiplied by \(-2\)?
content.hint: Locate \(-6\) and \(-14\) on a number line. The number farther right is greater.
content.explanation: The order reverses: \(-6>-14\). Multiplication by a negative reflects both values across zero.
content.solution: Multiply: \(3(-2)=-6\) and \(7(-2)=-14\). Since \(-6\) is greater than \(-14\), the true comparison is \(-6>-14\).

blocks.html:
Reverse only for a negative multiplier or divisor

Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative reverses their order. Flip the inequality sign at that step. Adding, subtracting, or multiplying or dividing by a positive keeps its direction.

content.prompt: During which step must the inequality sign reverse?
choices: Subtracting 8 from both sides
Dividing both sides by 4
Adding \(-3\) to both sides
Dividing both sides by \(-5\)
content.hint: Look for multiplication or division whose factor is negative.
content.explanation: Dividing by \(-5\) triggers the flip. Adding a negative number is still addition, so it does not.
content.solution: Only choice D divides both sides by a negative number. That operation reverses the order of the values and therefore reverses the inequality.

blocks.html:
Isolate and keep the boundary

  1. Isolate the variable with equation moves.
  2. Reverse the sign if you multiply or divide by a negative.
  3. Read the allowed range; test an easy value if you want reassurance.

The boundary is the value at equality. < and > exclude it; ≤ and ≥ include it.

Follow one example

For \(-3x+7\ge22\), subtract 7 to get \(-3x\ge15\). Divide by -3 and reverse: \(x\le-5\).

The boundary -5 is included. As a quick check, -6 makes the original statement true.

content.hint: Subtract 5, then divide by \(-2\). That last step has the flip trigger.
content.explanation: Subtracting gives \(-2x<12\). Divide by \(-2\), reverse the sign, and get \(x>-6\).
content.solution: \(5-2x<17\Rightarrow-2x<12\Rightarrow x>-6\). A check such as \(x=0\) makes the original statement \(5<17\), which is true.

blocks.html:
Ask whether equality counts

“At least” includes the minimum: ≥. “At most” includes the maximum: ≤. “More than” and “fewer than” exclude the boundary: > and <.

Use that distinction to translate a budget or limit.

shared_prompt.title: Theater ticket budget
shared_prompt.html: A theater charges $12 per ticket plus a one-time $8 fee. Priya can spend no more than $80. Let \(t\) be the number of tickets.

content.prompt: Which inequality models the ticket budget?
content.hint: The $12 charge repeats for each ticket; the $8 fee happens once. Can the total equal $80?
content.explanation: \(12t+8\leq80\). The SAT's traps either reverse “no more than” or put the one-time fee inside the repeated charge.
content.solution: Tickets cost \(12t\), and the fee adds 8, so the total is \(12t+8\). No more than $80 means the total may equal 80 but cannot exceed it: \(12t+8\leq80\).

content.prompt: Using \(12t+8\leq80\), what is the greatest possible number of tickets Priya can buy?
content.hint: Subtract 8 and divide by 12. Then remember that a ticket count must be a whole number.
content.explanation: The inequality gives \(t\leq6\), so 6 is the greatest possible whole-number ticket count.
content.solution: \(12t+8\leq80\Rightarrow12t\leq72\Rightarrow t\leq6\). Therefore, the greatest possible number is 6.

blocks.html:
A solution can be a pair

For a two-variable inequality, a pair works when substituting both coordinates makes the statement true. For \(2x+y<7\), the pair \((2,1)\) gives 5<7, so it works.

content.prompt: Which ordered pair is a solution to \(3x-2y\geq4\)?
content.hint: Substitute each x-coordinate for \(x\) and its matching y-coordinate for \(y\). Look for a result at least 4.
content.explanation: For \((2,1)\), \(3(2)-2(1)=4\), and equality is allowed by \(\geq\).
content.solution: The left sides are \(-2,-1,4,-1\), respectively. Only 4 is greater than or equal to 4, so \((2,1)\) works.

blocks.html:
Substitute, Simplify, Compare

  1. Put the first coordinate into x and the second into y.
  2. Calculate both sides.
  3. Decide whether the inequality is true.

If a table claims all its rows work, check every row. One false row eliminates the table.

content.prompt: A table lists \((-1,2)\), \((0,3)\), and \((2,5)\). Do all three pairs satisfy \(y\geq x+3\)?
choices: Yes; each row makes the inequality true.
No; the first row makes the inequality false.
No; the second row makes the inequality false.
No; the third row makes the inequality false.
content.hint: Check the rows one at a time: compare each y-value with its x-value plus 3.
content.explanation: All three land on the boundary: \(2=-1+3\), \(3=0+3\), and \(5=2+3\). The \(\geq\) sign includes equality.
content.solution: Substitution produces \(2\geq2\), \(3\geq3\), and \(5\geq5\). Every statement is true, so every row is a solution.

blocks.html:
A graph shows the allowed region

Use equality for the boundary line. A dashed line excludes its points; a solid line includes them.

Test a point off the line. If it makes the inequality true, shade its side. For \(y>2x-1\), that is the region above a dashed boundary.

content.prompt: Which description matches the graph of \(y<-x+4\)?
choices: A solid boundary with the region above it shaded
A dashed boundary with the region below it shaded
A dashed boundary with the region above it shaded
A solid boundary with the region below it shaded
content.hint: First decide whether equality is included. Then test \((0,0)\): is \(0<4\) true?
content.explanation: The strict sign makes the boundary dashed. Since \((0,0)\) satisfies the inequality and lies below the line, shade below.
content.solution: The boundary \(y=-x+4\) is dashed because \(<\) excludes equality. The test point \((0,0)\) gives \(0<4\), so shade the side containing the origin: below the line.

blocks.html:
Return to the integer question

Try the opening inequality again. Track which values are allowed, then report the kind of value the question asks for.

content.prompt: Return to the opening question. What answer do you get now?
content.hint: Expand the parentheses and isolate x. Dividing by a negative reverses the sign. Then choose the greatest integer in the allowed range.
content.explanation: The inequality simplifies to \(11-8x>27\), then \(-8x>16\), so \(x<-2\). The greatest integer below \(-2\) is \(-3\).
content.solution: The inequality simplifies to \(11-8x>27\), then \(-8x>16\), so \(x<-2\). The greatest integer below \(-2\) is \(-3\).

content.prompt: The Boundary and Test move has to survive test day. Which routine keeps both one- and two-variable inequalities honest?
choices: Isolate the variable, flip after subtraction, and test a pair by substituting both coordinates.
Isolate the variable, keep the sign after negative division, and test a pair by substituting both coordinates.
Isolate the variable, flip after negative multiplication or division, and test a pair by substituting both coordinates.
Isolate the variable, flip after positive division, and test a pair by substituting both coordinates.
content.explanation: That is Boundary and Test: protect the sign during isolation, then substitute into the original statement. For a table, every claimed pair must pass.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: Which ordered pair does not satisfy \(2x+3y\leq12\)?
content.explanation: \((2,3)\) gives \(2(2)+3(3)=13\), which is not at most 12. Each other pair gives exactly 12.

content.prompt: A delivery service charges a one-time fee of $18 plus $6 for each package. A customer can spend at most $75. What is the greatest number of packages the customer can send?
content.explanation: \(18+6p\leq75\) gives \(p\leq9.5\). Packages come in whole numbers, so the greatest possible count is 9—not the decimal boundary.

content.html:
Boundary and Test

Track equality, reverse on negative multiplication or division, and answer in context.
